overview: Computer Science is the sharpest available test of whether "oversubscribed programme" always means "structurally different" in this package, because global CS demand surged recently and on top of admissions architectures mostly designed decades before anyone needed a CS-specific gate. This package's Medicine document found a structurally different mechanism in 13 of 15 countries. Computer Science inverts that ratio: across the 15 countries researched here, Computer Science runs through the country's own general admissions mechanism -- the same threshold, formula, ranking system, or points calculation used for any other popular degree -- in 10 of 15 cases, with selectivity expressed purely as an extreme, demand-driven cutoff (Turkey, Spain, Ireland, France, Italy, Australia, New Zealand, Hong Kong, Singapore, Canada). This is the "numerically stricter only" pattern this research brief anticipated as the dominant shape for a globally oversubscribed field, and the anticipation held for two-thirds of the countries in this document -- the majority pattern, not a null result. The genuine exceptions are informative precisely because they are a minority, and precisely because none of them are CS-specific inventions -- each rides an admissions mechanism the country already had for other purposes, which Computer Science now happens to trigger because of demand. The United States shows the sharpest and most consequential structural split: at a meaningful subset of top public and private universities, Computer Science is not one admissions object but either a direct-admit school-within-the-university evaluated separately and far more harshly at the point of first application (UC Berkeley's EECS, Carnegie Mellon's School of Computer Science), or a field a student can be admitted to the university without being admitted to, requiring a separate, competitive, sometimes post-matriculation internal gate (Berkeley's own L&S/CDSS Computer Science major, the University of Washington's Allen School). The United Kingdom and the Netherlands each show a real but narrower structural difference: the UK layers a mandatory admissions-test requirement (TMUA, plus an additional college-specific test at two Cambridge colleges) onto general admission's grades-and-personal-statement model, though this layer is shared with other quantitative subjects, not unique to CS; the Netherlands lets each university independently decide whether Computer Science is numerus fixus at all, producing TU Delft's tested, capacity-capped Computer Science & Engineering sitting alongside the University of Amsterdam's uncapped Informatica for the identically-named field. Germany adds a third, subtler version of the same idea: Computer Science never triggers Germany's heaviest national NC architecture (reserved for exactly four subjects, none of them CS), but at the university level it ranges from fully open (RWTH Aachen, confirmed zulassungsfrei) to a standard local-NC grade-plus-criteria threshold (KIT) to a dedicated qualitative aptitude/suitability-assessment procedure (TU Munich's Eignungsfeststellungsverfahren). Switzerland supplies a useful negative-control finding: Computer Science at ETH Zurich and most Swiss universities carries no numerus clausus of any kind -- the sole confirmed exception in Swiss admissions is human medicine -- and CS's real difficulty there is an informal, brutal first year, not a documented admissions gate.

countries.scope: university-specific -- not a national rule; concentrated at large public flagships (Berkeley, Washington) and a subset of elite privates (Carnegie Mellon) that use either direct-admit-by-college or a post-matriculation internal-major gate
countries.description: Not one national mechanism, and not universal -- most US universities simply let a student declare Computer Science as an ordinary major with no special gate. Where it does apply, two genuinely different shapes were confirmed. Direct-admit school-within-the-university: UC Berkeley's EECS is a College of Engineering major admitted directly and bindingly at the point of freshman application (acceptance commonly cited under 5%); Berkeley's own EECS page states that admissions processes for EECS/Electrical & Computer Engineering (College of Engineering) versus Computer Science (College of Computing, Data Science and Society, formerly under Letters & Sciences) "vary significantly" even though the technical CS coursework is nearly identical. Carnegie Mellon admits every applicant into one of seven colleges at first application, not to the university generally -- the School of Computer Science (SCS) admits under 5%, versus roughly 24% for Dietrich College -- and CMU's own admissions materials confirm SCS is the only college requiring a mandatory SAT/ACT score for Fall 2026 applicants while sibling colleges are test-flexible or test-optional. Admitted-to-the-university-without-admission-to-the-major: Berkeley's own high-demand-major policy (now governing CS under CDSS) guarantees a place in a declared high-demand major only for students who selected it on their initial application; a student admitted via a different major or undeclared status gets just "one opportunity" to apply into CS later, at "extremely limited" odds. The University of Washington's Allen School runs this shape even more explicitly: a "Direct to Major" pathway is evaluated at first application (roughly 2-5% of non-resident applicants, 26-37% of resident applicants per the Allen School's own published data), alongside a wholly separate "Current UW Student Admission" pathway -- its own departmental application, CS-specific essay prompts, minimum prerequisite coursework graded 2.0+ -- that remains genuinely competitive (24% of Washington residents, 37% of non-residents/international applicants, Spring/Autumn 2025 cycles) even though every applicant is already a currently-enrolled UW student.
countries.eligibility_determinants: Which specific university/college a student applies to, since that determines whether a separate, harder admissions pool applies at first application (Berkeley EECS, CMU SCS) or whether general university admission alone is sufficient to enter the CS major (most US universities); at direct-admit schools, demonstrated math/CS coursework rigor and, at CMU SCS specifically, a mandatory SAT/ACT score; for students admitted without a declared CS major at a two-gate school, completed prerequisite coursework at a minimum grade threshold for the internal/secondary application.
countries.strengthens_application: At direct-admit schools: AP Computer Science A, AP Calculus BC, and demonstrated independent programming/competition experience (USACO, hackathons, open-source contributions, research) -- named specifically in the Allen School's own published admit profile. At two-gate schools for a student seeking the internal transfer: the strongest possible grade performance in the specific prerequisite course sequence (UW requires 2.0+ in each; competitive admits run well above that).
countries.largely_irrelevant: General extracurricular breadth unconnected to demonstrated computing/mathematics depth; a CS-specific supplemental essay at CMU distinct from its standard shared three-essay set -- not confirmed to exist in sources reviewed.
countries.never_infer: Never treat "EECS" and "Computer Science" -- or any two similarly CS-adjacent major names at the same US university -- as interchangeable or as sharing one admissions pathway; Berkeley's own site states its admissions processes for the two "vary significantly." Never assume a US applicant admitted to a university has thereby been admitted to that university's Computer Science major -- true at only a subset of US universities, never assume it generalizes nationally. Never repeat the CMU School-of-Computer-Science separate-supplemental-essay claim as confirmed fact -- it was a lead this research was asked to verify and was not found in CMU's own admissions materials.

countries.scope: national instrument (TMUA, required university-wide for CS at several institutions) + college-specific supplement (CSAT, Cambridge's Peterhouse and Trinity colleges only)
countries.description: TMUA (Test of Mathematics for University Admission) is mandatory for Cambridge Computer Science and Imperial Computing for current-cycle entry, confirmed directly via both departments' own admissions pages. Imperial's own course page confirms it no longer uses MAT (Mathematics Admissions Test), which it required historically -- a dated, confirmed change. TMUA is also used by Warwick, Durham, UCL, and LSE for various quantitative courses (Mathematics, Economics, some Statistics), so this testing layer is shared across quantitative subjects generally, not exclusive to CS. Cambridge adds one further, narrower layer: the Computer Science Aptitude Test (CSAT) is required only for applicants to two named colleges, Peterhouse and Trinity, as an additional test sat on top of the university-wide TMUA requirement -- confirmed directly via Cambridge's Computer Science and Technology department's own admissions pages. This is a real difference from general non-quantitative UK admission (predicted grades, one shared personal statement, one shared school reference, rarely an interview) but should not be described as one Cambridge-wide "Computer Science admissions assessment" replacing TMUA -- it is TMUA university-wide, plus CSAT at exactly two colleges.
countries.eligibility_determinants: A-Level/IB/equivalent grades meeting the specific department's threshold, plus a TMUA sitting (registered in advance, ahead of the UCAS deadline), plus, only for Peterhouse/Trinity applicants, a CSAT sitting.
countries.strengthens_application: A strong TMUA score (2025-entry successful Imperial applicants commonly scored around 5.5+, though Imperial states no fixed threshold); strong CSAT performance for the two colleges that require it; demonstrated subject-adjacent depth (Computer Science, Further Mathematics, Physics named as recommended subjects at Imperial) referenced in the personal statement.
countries.largely_irrelevant: General breadth of extracurriculars unconnected to mathematics/computing; multiple personal recommendation letters -- the UK uses one shared school reference for every choice, CS included.
countries.never_infer: Never assume MAT is still current for Imperial Computing -- it has been replaced by TMUA. Never describe CSAT as a Cambridge-wide requirement -- it applies only to Peterhouse and Trinity applicants, on top of the university-wide TMUA. Never assume TMUA cutoffs are nationally uniform -- they are set per department/college.

countries.scope: university-specific -- the 2023 national numerus fixus law lets each institution decide whether to invoke it at all for Computer Science, confirmed to differ for the identical field between TU Delft (capped) and UvA (uncapped) in the same 2026-27 cycle
countries.description: Genuinely varies by university for the identical named field, confirmed for the current cycle. TU Delft's Computer Science & Engineering is numerus fixus: 590 places for 2026-27 (345 English-track, 245 bilingual Dutch-English track), using a mandatory Mathematics + Systematic Reasoning test to stratify applicants into ranked bands before a within-band placement decision. The University of Amsterdam's Informatica, confirmed directly via UvA's own admissions page, is NOT numerus fixus at all -- subject only to UvA's standard "Matching" participation requirement (mandatory, but not a competitive-selection gate; failing to complete it leads to deregistration, not rejection). This is the same finding shape already established for Medicine in this package (institution-varying selection method under the 2023 numerus fixus law), but the axis here is starker: whether the field is capacity-restricted at all, not merely which method applies once it is.
countries.eligibility_determinants: VWO Natuur & Techniek (or foreign equivalent, e.g. Mathematics B-level, Physics) establishes general eligibility; at TU Delft specifically, the Mathematics + Systematic Reasoning test result then determines ranked-band placement; at UvA, completing Matching participation is the only additional gate.
countries.strengthens_application: At TU Delft: strong performance on the Mathematics + Systematic Reasoning test. At UvA and other non-numerus-fixus Informatica programmes: nothing beyond meeting the VWO-equivalence and subject-prerequisite baseline, since there is no ranking to improve position within.
countries.largely_irrelevant: General extracurricular breadth; recommendation letters, which are not a Dutch feature at any level, Computer Science included.
countries.never_infer: Never describe "the Dutch Computer Science selection method" as one national mechanism, or even as consistently numerus fixus -- TU Delft and UvA run genuinely different regimes (capped-and-tested vs. uncapped) for the identically-named field in the same cycle. Never assume this year's status at a given university persists next cycle -- institutions can and do switch under the 2023 law's permitted options.

countries.scope: university-specific, entirely within the local NC layer -- Computer Science never enters national NC; confirmed to range from open (RWTH Aachen) to standard local NC (KIT) to a dedicated qualitative assessment procedure (TU Munich) for the identical field
countries.description: Computer Science never enters Germany's heaviest national mechanism -- hochschulstart's centrally-coordinated NC allocation applies to exactly four subjects (Medicine, Dentistry, Veterinary Medicine, Pharmacy), and CS was not found on that list at any point in sources reviewed. At the university level, however, confirmed sources show three genuinely different mechanisms for the identically-named Bachelor's field. RWTH Aachen's Informatik B.Sc. is confirmed zulassungsfrei (admission-free, no local NC) for winter semester 2026/27, directly per RWTH's own programme page. KIT's Informatik B.Sc. is confirmed zulassungsbeschraenkt (443 places, local NC) per KIT's own published programme flyer -- structurally the standard Baden-Wuerttemberg local-NC shape (a grade-based criterion plus at least one non-grade criterion, per state regulation). TU Munich's Bachelor Informatik uses neither of those: TUM's own programme page states directly that student selection runs through an "Eignungsfeststellungsverfahren" -- a qualitative, multi-stage aptitude/suitability-assessment procedure, structurally distinct from a plain grade-rank local NC and closer in kind to the Netherlands' decentralized-qualitative-selection Medicine universities than to a typical German local NC. Fully open, standard local NC, and a dedicated qualitative assessment procedure are three different mechanisms operating on one field, at three of Germany's most CS-reputable universities, inside one country.
countries.eligibility_determinants: Abiturnote (or recognized equivalent) is sufficient alone at zulassungsfrei universities (e.g. RWTH Aachen); at standard local-NC universities (e.g. KIT), Abiturnote plus the university's chosen non-grade criterion determine ranked placement; at TU Munich, completion and result of the Eignungsfeststellungsverfahren determines admission independent of a simple grade rank.
countries.strengthens_application: At TU Munich specifically: strong performance in the Eignungsfeststellungsverfahren's assessment stages. At standard local-NC universities: the same levers that help any German local-NC applicant -- strongest possible Abiturnote plus whatever non-grade criterion that specific university has chosen to weight.
countries.largely_irrelevant: General leadership, non-CS extracurriculars, essays, and recommendation letters -- absent from the German Computer Science pipeline as they are from German admission generally, at all three university types identified.
countries.never_infer: Never assume one German university's Informatik admission mechanism (open, local-NC, or aptitude-assessed) generalizes to a different German university for the identical field -- confirmed variation across RWTH, KIT, and TUM makes the country-level fact close to unusable on its own. Never assume Computer Science triggers Germany's national NC quota system the way Medicine does -- it does not, at any university identified.

countries.scope: local/university (numero chiuso locale via TOL/TOLC-I), never the national numero chiuso track reserved for Medicine/Dentistry/Vet Med
countries.description: Runs entirely through Italy's already-documented local numero chiuso track -- never the national one, which is reserved for Medicine, Dentistry, and Veterinary Medicine -- using the same CISIA TOL/TOLC-I test family used for many other high-demand degrees. Confirmed at Politecnico di Milano (TOL test, minimum 30 points required, capped attempts per cycle) and Sapienza (TOLC-I, English TOLC-I, or TOLC-CASA for its limited/programmed-admission engineering degrees, which include Informatica). Same mechanism and same instrument family as the general Italian local-track pattern already documented generally -- Computer Science is one of the fields that reliably triggers it given demand, not a new mechanism.
countries.eligibility_determinants: Secondary diploma meeting the 12-year threshold, plus a TOL/TOLC-I (or CEnT-S at universities that have adopted the newer unified test) score that clears that specific university's locally-set ranking threshold for that cycle.
countries.strengthens_application: Strong TOL/TOLC-I preparation and score -- the same lever as any other locally-capped Italian engineering/technical degree.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Personal statements, recommendation letters, general extracurricular review -- absent from Italy's admission architecture generally, Computer Science included.
countries.never_infer: Never assume Computer Science is governed by Italy's national numero chiuso (Medicine/Dentistry/Vet Med only) -- it is a local/university-level capacity decision, varying institution-by-institution and year-by-year. Never assume a TOL score threshold at one university transfers to another.

countries.scope: university/faculty-level -- rides Canada's already-documented separate-faculty-application model; Waterloo's Cheriton School of Computer Science sits in the Faculty of Mathematics, evaluated differently in detail (no interview) from Waterloo Engineering (AIF plus interview) at the same institution
countries.description: Rides Canada's already-documented "separate faculty/programme application" model rather than introducing anything new. University of Waterloo, the sharpest and most internationally-recognized example, places Computer Science inside the Faculty of Mathematics (Cheriton School of Computer Science) rather than Engineering: applicants submit an Admission Information Form (AIF) covering courses, non-academic activities, and math-contest participation -- confirmed directly via the Cheriton School's own admissions page, contest participation (Canadian Computing Competition, Euclid, Canadian Senior Mathematics Contest) is explicitly not required and mainly helps borderline applicants -- but, also confirmed directly, no interview is used for Computer Science admission, unlike Waterloo Engineering, which layers an AIF plus a mandatory online interview plus supplementary forms on top of its own five-course prerequisite set. This is university-level texture inside Canada's existing general mechanism, not a new structural category nationally.
countries.eligibility_determinants: Senior secondary grades/admission average meeting the programme's threshold, plus a completed AIF (courses, non-academic activities, math contests, other information) -- no interview for Computer Science specifically at Waterloo, unlike Waterloo Engineering.
countries.strengthens_application: Strong admission average; a well-completed AIF describing relevant activities and any math-contest participation, though contests are explicitly optional; demonstrated programming/project experience described within the AIF.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Formal interviews and essays in the US sense -- Waterloo's AIF replaces a personal statement, and no interview applies to Computer Science the way one does for Waterloo Engineering.
countries.never_infer: Never assume Computer Science at a Canadian university uses the identical admission process as Engineering at that same university -- confirmed different at Waterloo specifically (no interview for CS vs. AIF-plus-interview for Engineering). Never assume math-contest results are required -- Waterloo states directly they are not.

countries.scope: national pattern (absence of NC) -- confirmed no numerus clausus for Computer Science at ETH Zurich or, per swissuniversities, almost any Swiss field outside human medicine
countries.description: The clearest disconfirming case in this document. ETH Zurich's own admissions materials and swissuniversities' national reference both indicate no numerus clausus applies to Computer Science (or almost any field) in Switzerland -- the one confirmed exception across sources reviewed, repeated consistently, is human medicine. A Swiss-Matura holder's route into ETH Zurich Informatik is the same automatic-threshold model as any other Bachelor's field; a foreign-diploma holder sits the same general ETH entrance examination (reduced or comprehensive, depending on prior qualification) that any non-automatically-recognized applicant to any ETH field would sit -- nothing CS-specific about it. Computer Science's genuine, well-known difficulty at ETH is realized almost entirely through informal first-year academic attrition rather than through any documented admissions gate -- a structurally different kind of "hard to get into" than every other country in this document.
countries.eligibility_determinants: Matura (or a recognized-equivalent foreign diploma clearing the direct-admission threshold); for non-automatically-recognized foreign qualifications, the general ETH entrance examination (reduced or comprehensive) -- identical to the eligibility path for most other ETH Bachelor's fields, not a CS-specific gate.
countries.strengthens_application: Nothing beyond meeting the same Matura-equivalence/entrance-exam threshold any other non-Medicine ETH Bachelor's applicant needs to meet -- there is no ranking or selection process to improve position within at the admissions stage.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Personal statements, recommendation letters, general extracurricular review, and any CS-specific aptitude test -- none apply, consistent with Swiss Bachelor's admission generally outside Medicine.
countries.never_infer: Never model Switzerland's genuine Computer Science difficulty as an admissions-eligibility fact the way EMS or numerus fixus is modeled for Swiss Medicine -- it is a post-entry, first-year academic-attrition phenomenon, not a documented admissions gate, and treating it as one would misrepresent the actual mechanism to a student or counselor.

countries.scope: national frameworks already documented generally (licence-en-tension under loi ORE; CPGE-to-concours), applied to CS-labeled tracks (ordinary Licence Informatique; the MP2I/MPI CPGE track) rather than a new mechanism
countries.description: Runs through the two mechanisms the general France document already established, with no CS-specific third mechanism found. Ordinary Licence Informatique at popular universities functions as a "licence en tension" under the 2018 loi ORE -- the same attendus-fit ranking layer already documented for Droit/STAPS/Psychologie/Eco-gestion -- now also reported at extreme oversubscription (one cited example: roughly 5,600 Parcoursup applications for 145 places at a single Paris-area university's Informatique programme). The elite quantitative track into engineering Grandes Ecoles runs through the same CPGE-to-concours mechanism already documented generally, using a CS-flavored prepa track (MP2I in the first year, feeding into MPI in the second, alongside the older MPSI/MP track) rather than a separate admissions architecture -- a track label change, not a new mechanism. MP2I/MPI selectivity varies enormously by lycee (low in the provinces, extreme at Paris's most reputed CPGE classes), mirroring the country document's own finding that CPGE selectivity is genuinely local, not nationally uniform.
countries.eligibility_determinants: Holding the Bac (or a DAP-track equivalent) is sufficient for ordinary Licence Informatique consideration; attendus-fit (spécialités retained through terminale, commonly Mathématiques) determines ranking when the specific university's Informatique programme is in tension; CPGE entry for the MP2I/MPI track is dossier-based via Parcoursup, with the real bottleneck at the concours two years later.
countries.strengthens_application: For Licence Informatique en tension: strong attendus-aligned terminale performance, particularly in Mathématiques. For the CPGE-MP2I/MPI-to-Grande-Ecole route: strong CPGE academic performance feeding into the concours, which is the actual competitive filter, not CPGE entry itself.
countries.largely_irrelevant: The Parcoursup 'projet de formation motive' motivation text carries the same limited, non-exclusionary role documented generally for France; general extracurricular evidence has no confirmed role in either mechanism.
countries.never_infer: Never treat MP2I/MPI as a separate admissions architecture from France's general CPGE-to-concours mechanism -- it is a track label within that same mechanism. Never treat Licence Informatique's 'en tension' status as uniform nationally -- it varies by university and cycle like any other tension licence.

countries.scope: national formula (ponderación/nota de corte/Distrito Único), uniform mechanism, extreme university-specific emergent cutoffs at UPC/UPM
countries.description: Runs through the identical ponderación/nota de corte/Distrito Unico mechanism used for every other public Grado programme, with an extreme, self-adjusting cutoff at the most in-demand schools: Ingenieria Informatica's illustrative 2025-26/projected 2026 cutoffs sit above roughly 10.5 out of 14 at both UPC's Facultat d'Informatica de Barcelona and UPM -- a range comparable to several public Medicine cutoffs documented in this package's Medicine research. No dedicated test, portfolio, or interview layer was found for the public track -- the same mechanism as any other competitive Spanish Grado, just with an extreme emergent cutoff.
countries.eligibility_determinants: The same EBAU/Bachillerato-based nota de acceso/nota de admision (plus ponderación subject bonuses, commonly Mathematics and Physics for Informática) as any other Grado programme, ranked via Distrito Único.
countries.strengthens_application: Maximizing EBAU voluntary-phase weighted-subject scores (ponderación, typically Matemáticas II and Física for Informática) and Bachillerato average -- the same levers as any competitive Grado, just against a much higher bar.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Personal statements, recommendation letters, extracurricular activities -- absent from the public formula entirely.
countries.never_infer: Never assume Spanish public Ingeniería Informática has any hidden interview, portfolio, or aptitude-test gate beyond the EBAU/nota-de-corte mechanism -- sources reviewed found none. Never treat one cycle's illustrative cutoff figure as predictive of a future cycle's self-adjusting nota de corte.

countries.scope: national (CAO points formula), uniform across all HEIs reviewed, no second instrument found for Computer Science anywhere
countries.description: Runs entirely through ordinary CAO Leaving Certificate points, with no HPAT-style second instrument, portfolio, or interview found for Computer Science at either Trinity or UCD -- despite Computer Science carrying some of the highest points requirements in the country (Trinity's Computer Science course reported by Trinity's own school as the highest-points CS degree in Ireland in the 2025 cycle; UCD Computer Science required 542 points in Round 1 of the same cycle, both well above 500 and approaching the 625-point maximum). The Higher Level Mathematics +25-point bonus that applies generally across the Irish system is the only Mathematics-specific lever available, not a Computer-Science-specific one -- and CAO's own "restricted-application course" category (used for Medicine, Art & Design/Architecture-type portfolio courses) does not name Computer Science.
countries.eligibility_determinants: Leaving Certificate points (best 6 subjects, plus the national Higher Level Mathematics +25-point bonus where earned) meeting that programme's current-cycle points requirement -- no additional test or instrument.
countries.strengthens_application: Maximizing Leaving Certificate points in the highest-weighted subjects, particularly securing the Higher Level Mathematics bonus -- the same lever as any other points-based course, just against one of the highest bars nationally.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Essays, recommendation letters, general extracurricular review, portfolios, and interviews -- structurally absent from the CAO points route for Computer Science, as for most non-restricted courses.
countries.never_infer: Never assume Computer Science carries a second scored instrument the way Medicine's HPAT does -- none was found at either Trinity or UCD. Never assume a high published points requirement implies a different mechanism -- it is the same points-only mechanism, just an extreme emergent cutoff.

countries.scope: university-specific floating ATAR/selection-rank threshold, the same mechanism used for the large majority of Australian programmes
countries.description: Runs through the same floating ATAR/selection-rank mechanism used for the large majority of Australian programmes, with published guide ATAR figures spanning roughly 75-82 at mid-tier universities up to 85-95 for Advanced Computing-style degrees at Group of Eight universities. No Commonwealth-Supported-Place-style fixed government place allocation (the specific mechanism that makes Medicine categorically different in Australia) and no UCAT ANZ/ISAT-style dedicated admissions test or interview was found for Computer Science in sources reviewed. Mathematical Methods is commonly a named prerequisite or strongly assumed-knowledge subject at Go8 universities, consistent with the general prerequisite/assumed-knowledge distinction already documented for Australia broadly -- not a CS-specific mechanism.
countries.eligibility_determinants: ATAR or selection rank meeting that cycle's floating cutoff, plus Mathematical Methods as a stated prerequisite or assumed-knowledge subject at most Go8 universities.
countries.strengthens_application: Mathematical Methods completion and strong performance where it is a stated prerequisite rather than merely assumed knowledge; ATAR/selection-rank maximization generally -- no CS-specific lever beyond the general Australian admissions model.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Portfolios, interviews, dedicated admissions tests, and CSP-style place-count guarantees -- none apply to Computer Science the way they do to Medicine in Australia.
countries.never_infer: Never assume Computer Science benefits from Medicine's government-allocated fixed Commonwealth Supported Place mechanism -- CSP funding for CS follows the general dollars-based, university-discretion model, not Medicine's fixed-place-count exception. Never treat 'assumed knowledge' Mathematical Methods as equivalent to a hard prerequisite -- the distinction is university- and programme-specific.

countries.scope: university-specific Rank Score/grade-average threshold, the same mechanism used for most NZ Bachelor's programmes
countries.description: Runs through the same Rank Score/grade-average threshold mechanism used for most New Zealand Bachelor's programmes, with quantitative programmes commonly expecting Level 3 Calculus and/or Physics from the shared national UE-approved-subjects list. No UCAT ANZ-style dedicated test, and no two-stage gateway-then-competitive-progression model of the kind confirmed for NZ Medicine, was found for Computer Science in sources reviewed this pass -- a lower-confidence entry than most others in this document given the comparatively thin official-source material located.
countries.eligibility_determinants: University Entrance plus a graduated Rank Score (or programme-specific grade average) meeting that university's current threshold; Level 3 Calculus and/or Physics commonly expected for quantitative/STEM-adjacent programmes generally.
countries.strengthens_application: Strong Rank Score / NCEA credit accumulation in Calculus and Physics-adjacent subjects -- the same general lever as any competitive NZ Bachelor's programme.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Interviews, dedicated admissions tests, and two-stage gateway-then-progression structures -- none confirmed for Computer Science the way they are for NZ Medicine.
countries.never_infer: Never assume NZ Computer Science uses a UCAT-ANZ-style test or Medicine's gateway-year structure -- neither was found in sources reviewed. Treat this country's CS finding as lower-confidence than most others in this document given the thinner source base located this pass.

countries.scope: bifurcated by applicant type (JUPAS/non-JUPAS, per the general country finding) then university-specific within non-JUPAS (HKUST confirmed no interview; HKU unconfirmed)
countries.description: Sits inside the same JUPAS/non-JUPAS bifurcation already documented generally in this package (RULE-ADMISSIONS-013): every internationally-educated applicant, Turkish or otherwise, is categorically routed to non-JUPAS regardless of field. Within non-JUPAS, HKUST's own FAQ for non-JUPAS/non-local applicants states directly that an interview "is not a requirement" for its School of Engineering, which houses Computer Science -- a confirmed absence at HKUST specifically, unlike Medicine's confirmed Multiple Mini Interview/panel requirement at HKU and CUHK respectively. HKU's own Computer Science admissions page does not itself specify whether an interview applies to non-JUPAS CS applicants; this specific sub-question is an unresolved gap, not a confirmed absence.
countries.eligibility_determinants: Non-JUPAS transcript/qualification review against each university's published minimum for Computer Science, no dedicated test confirmed; Mathematics at Advanced Level commonly required for STEM-track admission (confirmed at HKUST).
countries.strengthens_application: Strong Mathematics performance (Advanced Level or HL-equivalent); meeting or exceeding the published minimum average for the applicant's specific qualification type at the target university.
countries.largely_irrelevant: A mandatory interview -- confirmed not required at HKUST specifically for Computer Science, unlike Medicine at HKU/CUHK; general extracurricular review beyond transcript/qualification minimums.
countries.never_infer: Never assume HKU Computer Science requires an interview the way HKU Medicine does -- HKU's own CS admissions page does not confirm this either way; treat as an open question, not an assumed yes or no. Never assume JUPAS is a viable route for an internationally-educated applicant to Computer Science -- it categorically is not, regardless of field.

countries.scope: university-specific (NUS holistic assessment; NTU IGP), both the same general mechanism used for most programmes at each AU, not Medicine's added ranking-gate/test layer
countries.description: This package's Medicine document confirmed NUS gates Medicine (and Dentistry, Law) with both a mandatory ranking-position rule (the field must be a top-1-or-2 ranked choice on the application) and a compulsory standardized-test layer (UCAT, or SAT/ACT-with-Writing plus AP Exams) that most NUS programmes do not carry. Computer Science carries neither. NUS Computing is evaluated through the same holistic-assessment mechanism (a structured achievements list, short-response questions) used for the large majority of NUS programmes, and NTU's Computer Science (College of Computing and Data Science) is evaluated through the same Integrated Grade Profile (IGP) mechanism used across NTU generally, with H2 Mathematics as a subject-level expectation rather than a dedicated test. Both are extremely selective by demand -- one ranking aggregator cites NUS Computer Science as the single most difficult NUS programme by admission difficulty (secondary-sourced, not an NUS-published figure); NTU CS's 10th-percentile IGP sits in the AAB/C band -- but the admission mechanism itself is the ordinary one used for most programmes, not Medicine's added ranking-gate-plus-test layer. SMU's specific CS mechanism was not independently confirmed to the same depth.
countries.eligibility_determinants: A-Level/IB/equivalent results meeting each AU's Integrated Grade Profile or holistic-review bar for Computer Science that cycle, with H2 Mathematics (NTU) or an equivalent strong quantitative subject expected; no mandatory standardized test or ranking-position rule confirmed the way Medicine/Law/Dentistry carry at NUS.
countries.strengthens_application: Strong H2/HL Mathematics performance; a well-completed structured achievements/CCA list at NUS (mandatory for every applicant to every programme, not CS-specific); IGP-maximizing grade performance at NTU.
countries.largely_irrelevant: A mandatory ranking-position placement of Computer Science among a student's top choices (unlike Medicine/Dentistry/Law at NUS); a mandatory UCAT/SAT-AP testing layer (unlike Medicine at NUS).
countries.never_infer: Never assume Singapore's Computer Science admission carries the same ranking-position gate or mandatory test layer that Medicine, Dentistry, and Law carry at NUS -- confirmed absent for CS at both NUS and NTU. Never treat a ranking aggregator's 'hardest NUS programme' claim as an NUS-published figure -- it is secondary-sourced.

countries.scope: national (YKS SAY score-type placement), uniform, no CS-specific layer at any Turkish university
countries.description: Bilgisayar Muhendisligi is placed entirely through the standard YKS SAY score-type mechanism -- the same formula, the same national rank-order competition, the same absence of interview or portfolio, as any other SAY-track engineering programme. What makes it 'restricted' is a cutoff near the top of the national distribution at the most reputable programmes: illustrative 2026-cycle figures place Bogazici's, Koc's, and Bilkent's Computer Engineering programmes within roughly the top 300-600 nationally by success ranking. No CS-specific mechanism of any kind was found -- the cleanest confirmation of 'numerically stricter only' in this document, matching Turkey's own Medicine finding in this package's Medicine document.
countries.eligibility_determinants: (TYT x 0.40) + (AYT x 0.60) + (OBP x 0.12 or 0.06) YKS SAY-type placement score, compared in strict national rank order against other candidates who listed the same programme code -- identical in kind to every other SAY-track lisans programme nationally.
countries.strengthens_application: Maximizing AYT Mathematics/Physics/Chemistry performance within the SAY score type -- the same lever as any other SAY-ranked engineering programme, just against a cutoff near the maximum attainable score at top-tier universities.
countries.largely_irrelevant: Essays, recommendation letters, interviews, portfolios, and extracurricular activities -- zero channel exists for any of these to matter in the domestic YKS pathway, Computer Engineering included.
countries.never_infer: Never assume Bilgisayar Muhendisligi has any non-score gate (interview, portfolio, aptitude test) -- none exists in the domestic pathway. Never assume a specific university's cutoff rank is stable cycle-to-cycle -- it is a self-adjusting, demand-driven figure recalculated each year.

cross_cutting_patterns: Unlike Medicine (structurally different in 13 of 15 countries), Computer Science is structurally different from a country's own general admissions model in only 4 of 15 countries researched (United States, United Kingdom, Netherlands, Germany), with a further country (Switzerland) confirmed to run CS through the SAME open mechanism as general admission -- more open, in a formal-admissions sense, than the country's own Medicine track. This confirms the research brief's hypothesis that CS's global oversubscription mostly manifests as 'numerically stricter,' not structurally different -- but the 4 genuine exceptions are concentrated in systems that already had a separate-college/school-within-university OR a per-institution-choice architecture available to apply to any oversubscribed field, not one built specifically for CS.

In the United States, CS-specific selectivity manifests in at least two textually different mechanisms within the same country, and a counselor must determine which one a target university uses before treating 'admitted to the university' as informative: (a) direct-admit into a separate, harder college/school evaluated at the point of first application (Berkeley EECS under 5%, CMU SCS under 5% with a mandatory-testing policy its peer colleges don't share) and (b) general-university admission followed by a distinct, competitive, sometimes post-matriculation internal-major gate (Berkeley L&S/CDSS CS's 'extremely limited' post-arrival switch odds; the University of Washington Allen School's Direct-to-Major vs. Current-UW-Student-Admission split, the latter admitting roughly 24-37% of an already-prerequisite-filtered pool). This sharpens the general US country document's own 'capacity-constrained major' finding with concrete, confirmed numbers, and is a genuinely different shape from Medicine's own US finding, since Medicine is not an undergraduate admissions object in the US at all while Computer Science is, and bifurcates into these two sub-mechanisms instead.

The same field can be open at one university and numerus-fixus-restricted at another within one country's identical formal legal framework: the Netherlands' 2023 numerus fixus law lets each institution decide whether to invoke it at all, and for Computer Science specifically this produces TU Delft's Computer Science & Engineering (numerus fixus, hybrid test-then-band selection, 590 places for 2026-27) sitting alongside the University of Amsterdam's Informatica (confirmed NOT numerus fixus) for the identically-named field, in the same cycle.

A country's Medicine mechanism and its Computer Science mechanism can point in genuinely opposite directions on the same structural axis, inside the same country: Singapore gates Medicine (and Dentistry/Law) with a mandatory ranking-position rule plus a compulsory standardized-test layer that most NUS programmes don't carry, but Computer Science at both NUS and NTU runs through the ordinary holistic/IGP review used for the large majority of programmes -- the same country, adjacent high-demand fields, opposite mechanism-type classification. A country's own general 'structurally different for X' finding must never be assumed to transfer to a different restricted field in that same country.

Where a country's general admissions model already contains a mechanism usable for ANY oversubscribed field (Canada's per-faculty application, the local-NC layer within Germany's own system), Computer Science's selectivity typically rides that pre-existing mechanism rather than introducing a new one -- but the SAME mechanism can still resolve differently at different institutions for the identical field, as confirmed for Germany (RWTH open vs. KIT standard local NC vs. TU Munich's dedicated qualitative Eignungsfeststellungsverfahren) -- a three-way split sharper than the simple open-vs-restricted binary the general German country document anticipated for local NC.

Switzerland is a genuine negative-control finding worth treating as its own mechanism_type value, not folded into 'numerically stricter only': ETH Zurich's and swissuniversities' own materials confirm no numerus clausus applies to Computer Science (or nearly any field) at all, human medicine being the sole confirmed exception -- meaning CS in Switzerland is not even numerically stricter in a formal-admissions sense, even though the field is informally notorious for a brutal first year. Modeling informal post-entry academic attrition as an admissions-eligibility fact would misrepresent the actual mechanism, and this distinction (formal admissions gate vs. informal post-entry difficulty) is itself a pattern worth tracking as its own field, separate from mechanism_type, in any future ORYN programme-requirement data model.
unresolved_questions: Germany: whether TU Munich's Eignungsfeststellungsverfahren-based Informatik selection is representative of other TUM CS-adjacent programmes (e.g. Data Engineering and Analytics, Games Engineering) or specific to the core Informatik Bachelor's was not checked this pass; whether KIT's Informatik local-NC criteria include a specific non-grade component beyond the Baden-Wuerttemberg-mandated general minimum was not independently confirmed for Informatik specifically.

United States: whether Carnegie Mellon's School of Computer Science carries any CS-specific supplemental essay prompt beyond CMU's standard shared three-essay set -- a specific sub-claim in this research's original brief -- was not confirmed in CMU's own admissions materials reviewed this pass; treated as unconfirmed rather than verified.

Hong Kong: whether HKU's Computer Science non-JUPAS pathway requires an interview, the way Medicine does at HKU and CUHK and the way HKUST's Engineering School confirms it does not for Computer Science, was not conclusively confirmed from HKU's own admissions pages this pass.

Singapore: SMU's specific Computer Science admission mechanism was not independently researched to the same depth as NUS's and NTU's this pass -- SMU's general 'SAT 1350 for most non-IB international qualifications' rule (documented in this package's country document) is assumed to apply by default, but no SMU-CS-specific added mechanism was checked for.

Netherlands: the full national list of which Informatica/Computer-Science-adjacent Bachelor's programmes beyond TU Delft (capped) and UvA (uncapped) currently use numerus fixus for the 2026-27 cycle -- e.g. Eindhoven University of Technology, Radboud, VU Amsterdam, Utrecht -- was not exhaustively mapped this pass.

Turkey: Istanbul Technical University's (ITU) and METU's specific 2026-cycle Bilgisayar Muhendisligi cutoff ranks were not directly confirmed this pass (Bogazici, Bilkent, and Koc were); their inclusion among 'top-tier, near-maximum cutoff' programmes rests on general reputational tier and the confirmed pattern at peer institutions, not independently verified rank data for these two specifically.

Australia: whether any Group of Eight university runs a CS-specific admissions test, portfolio, or interview layer (as opposed to a pure floating ATAR/selection-rank threshold) was not found in sources reviewed this pass -- read as a gap given this pass's depth, not a confirmed absence.

Ireland: whether any Irish HEI outside Trinity and UCD runs a CS-specific test or interview layer was not checked directly -- treated as likely-absent by pattern (CAO's own 'restricted-application course' category names Medicine and Art & Design/Architecture-type portfolio courses but not Computer Science), not exhaustively confirmed across every HEI offering the field.

New Zealand: this country's entry rests on a comparatively thin official-source base (ranking-aggregator and single-university sources rather than a national admissions body or multi-university primary confirmation) -- whether any NZ university runs a CS-specific test or two-stage structure was not confirmed to the same depth as most other countries in this document, and should be treated as the lowest-confidence entry here.
